sources.title: Potty Training
sources.quote: Don't make your child sit on the toilet against their will. ... Only put your child on the potty for a few minutes a couple of times a day, and let your child get up if he or she wants to. ... Have your child sit on the potty within 15 to 30 minutes after meals ... Avoid clothes that are hard to take off, such as overalls and shirts that snap in the crotch. ... follow the same routine and use the same names for body parts and bathroom acts ... tell your child that it was an accident and offer your support
sources.supports: No forcing, a few minutes a couple of times a day, sitting after meals and after waking dry, clothes that are easy to take off, the same words and routine for every caregiver, and support instead of disappointment after an accident.

sources.title: The Right Age to Potty Train
sources.quote: Asks to wear "big-kid" underwear ... Be a role model. Let your children see you use the toilet and wash your hands afterward. ... Children's feet should be able to reach the floor. ... Make a habit of seating your children onto the potty-chair first thing in the morning. ... Make sure both boys and girls learn to wash their hands well after using the toilet. ... Avoid treats and punishments. ... When your children succeed, be specific about why you are proud ... Avoid a power struggle.
sources.supports: Readiness signs, role model, a potty chair where the feet reach the floor, a morning routine, hand washing, specific praise instead of treats, and no power struggle. An AAP page (Adapted from Toilet Training, AAP 2022), applied to Israeli families as general child health advice.

sources.title: Potty Training: 12 Tips to Keep the Process Positive
sources.quote: Invite your child to take over their toileting. ... Avoid a power struggle. ... So power struggles, begging, pleading, rewarding, and punishing keep children from managing their own toileting. ... To give your children a feeling of control, let them flush the toilet. ... be specific about why you are proud
sources.supports: Invite the child to take over, avoid power struggles, let the child flush, and be specific about why you are proud. An AAP page (updated 11/6/2023).

sources.supports: Reading stories about feelings is one of the ways Zero To Three suggests to help a child with feelings. The page is about empathy; used only as support for stories about a hard moment, no promise of a result.

sources.title: The Right Age to Potty Train
sources.quote: Asks to wear "big-kid" underwear ... Be a role model. Let your children see you use the toilet and wash your hands afterward. ... Children's feet should be able to reach the floor. ... Make a habit of seating your children onto the potty-chair first thing in the morning. ... Make sure both boys and girls learn to wash their hands well after using the toilet. ... Avoid treats and punishments. ... When your children succeed, be specific about why you are proud ... Avoid a power struggle.
sources.supports: Readiness signs, role model, a potty chair where the feet reach the floor, a morning routine, hand washing, specific praise instead of treats, and no power struggle. An AAP page (Adapted from Toilet Training, AAP 2022), applied to Israeli families as general child health advice.

sources.title: Potty Training: 12 Tips to Keep the Process Positive
sources.quote: Invite your child to take over their toileting. ... Avoid a power struggle. ... So power struggles, begging, pleading, rewarding, and punishing keep children from managing their own toileting. ... To give your children a feeling of control, let them flush the toilet. ... be specific about why you are proud
sources.supports: Invite the child to take over, avoid power struggles, let the child flush, and be specific about why you are proud. An AAP page (updated 11/6/2023).

sources.title: Potty Training
sources.quote: Don't make your child sit on the toilet against their will. ... Only put your child on the potty for a few minutes a couple of times a day, and let your child get up if he or she wants to. ... Have your child sit on the potty within 15 to 30 minutes after meals ... Avoid clothes that are hard to take off, such as overalls and shirts that snap in the crotch. ... follow the same routine and use the same names for body parts and bathroom acts ... tell your child that it was an accident and offer your support
sources.supports: No forcing, a few minutes a couple of times a day, sitting after meals and after waking dry, clothes that are easy to take off, the same words and routine for every caregiver, and support instead of disappointment after an accident.

sources.title: Create a Potty Training Plan for Your Child
sources.quote: tell them you're sure they'll do better next time and ask them to help you clean up ... Try to be as consistent as possible.
sources.supports: After an accident, reassure the child and ask the child to help clean up; keep the routine consistent. Adapted from the AAP Guide to Toilet Training, 2nd edition (page updated 5/25/2022).

sources.title: Potty Training
sources.quote: Don't make your child sit on the toilet against their will. ... Only put your child on the potty for a few minutes a couple of times a day, and let your child get up if he or she wants to. ... Have your child sit on the potty within 15 to 30 minutes after meals ... Avoid clothes that are hard to take off, such as overalls and shirts that snap in the crotch. ... follow the same routine and use the same names for body parts and bathroom acts ... tell your child that it was an accident and offer your support
sources.supports: No forcing, a few minutes a couple of times a day, sitting after meals and after waking dry, clothes that are easy to take off, the same words and routine for every caregiver, and support instead of disappointment after an accident.

sources.title: The Right Age to Potty Train
sources.quote: Asks to wear "big-kid" underwear ... Be a role model. Let your children see you use the toilet and wash your hands afterward. ... Children's feet should be able to reach the floor. ... Make a habit of seating your children onto the potty-chair first thing in the morning. ... Make sure both boys and girls learn to wash their hands well after using the toilet. ... Avoid treats and punishments. ... When your children succeed, be specific about why you are proud ... Avoid a power struggle.
sources.supports: Readiness signs, role model, a potty chair where the feet reach the floor, a morning routine, hand washing, specific praise instead of treats, and no power struggle. An AAP page (Adapted from Toilet Training, AAP 2022), applied to Israeli families as general child health advice.

sources.title: Create a Potty Training Plan for Your Child
sources.quote: tell them you're sure they'll do better next time and ask them to help you clean up ... Try to be as consistent as possible.
sources.supports: After an accident, reassure the child and ask the child to help clean up; keep the routine consistent. Adapted from the AAP Guide to Toilet Training, 2nd edition (page updated 5/25/2022).

sources.title: Potty Training: 12 Tips to Keep the Process Positive
sources.quote: Invite your child to take over their toileting. ... Avoid a power struggle. ... So power struggles, begging, pleading, rewarding, and punishing keep children from managing their own toileting. ... To give your children a feeling of control, let them flush the toilet. ... be specific about why you are proud
sources.supports: Invite the child to take over, avoid power struggles, let the child flush, and be specific about why you are proud. An AAP page (updated 11/6/2023).

sources.title: How to Help Your Child Develop Empathy
sources.quote: Read stories about feelings.
sources.supports: Reading stories about feelings is one of the ways Zero To Three suggests to help a child with feelings. The page is about empathy; used only as support for stories about a hard moment, no promise of a result.

post_text.fb_text:
אני רואה איך אתם 🎒
מסתכלים בשעון
אני אלון, ובשבע וחצי הבית כבר רועש.
אני מחפש נעל, ואתם מסתכלים בשעון.
אני לא יודע לקרוא מחשבות,
אבל אני מרגיש אותן.
אז הנה מה שאני רוצה לענות.

״הוא מתעכב בכוונה״
אני עונה:
אני לא מרגיש איך הזמן עובר.
מה יעזור לי:
שעון שאני רואה, ומשפט כמו
״בשעה 7:20 לוקחים את התיק.״

״למה הוא לא מוכן כבר?״
אני עונה:
כי הכל נשאר לבוקר.
מה יעזור לי:
שבערב נשים בגדים ותיק ליד הדלת,
ואז בבוקר אין מה לחפש.

״צריך להעיר אותו בכוח״
מה אתם רואים:
ילד שנשאר במיטה.
מה קורה לי בפנים:
הצלצול חזק, ואני עוד עייף.
מה יעזור לי:
שיר שאני אוהב, או חיבוק.

״הוא שוכח משהו כל בוקר״
אני עונה:
יש לי הרבה דברים בראש.
מה יעזור לי:
בדיקה אחרונה: תיק, בקבוק, כריך.
ואולי שיר קטן שיזכיר לי.

״הוא פשוט עייף, זה יעבור״
אני עונה:
אני באמת צריך לישון מספיק.
מה יעזור לי:
לספור אחורה מהשעה שאני קם,
ולכבות מסכים שעה לפני השינה.

״מתי זה כבר יהיה רגוע?״
זה לא יקרה ביום אחד.
אבל כשיש סדר קבוע,
וגם אתם קמים קצת לפניי,
יש פחות ריצה בבוקר.
ואם נשאר זמן, נשחק משחק קטן.

אפשר גם לעזור להם
עם הבקרים הלחוצים
בעזרת ספר מותאם אישית.
תכתבו "כיתה"
ואשלח לכם קישור להכנת הספר 📖

sources.title: 8 ways to make school morning routines easier
sources.publisher: Understood (The Understood Team, expert review Donna Volpitta, EdD)
sources.quote: Start the night before. ... Wake up a little earlier than your child. ... Set your child's alarm to play a favorite song. ... Try waking your child up with lots of snuggles or a favorite breakfast. ... Follow the same routine before and after school. ... Make sure there are clocks "in your face" around the house. ... Give manageable countdowns, like "At 7:25, it'll be time to put your shoes on." ... Younger kids can come up with a silly phrase or song to help remember all the books and materials they need each morning. ... play a quick game together or read a book
sources.supports: Prepare the night before, parents wake a little earlier, a favorite song or snuggles instead of a jarring alarm, one routine, visible clocks with manageable countdowns, a double check, and a quick game if there is time to spare. A US page for families, applied as general advice.

sources.title: Back to School (for Parents)
sources.quote: Organize and set out what they need the night before. Homework and books should be put in their backpacks by the door and clothes should be laid out in their bedrooms. ... Consistent bedtime routines go a long way in helping kids have a great day at school.
sources.supports: Set out clothes and the backpack by the door the night before; a consistent bedtime routine.

sources.title: Sleep and Your School-Aged Child
sources.quote: School-age kids need 9–12 hours of sleep a night. ... Turn off all screens at least 1 hour before bedtime. ... decide when your child needs to get up for school in the morning and count back 9–12 hours from there
sources.supports: School-age children need 9 to 12 hours of sleep, count back from the wake-up time, and screens go off an hour before bed.

sources.quote: Read stories about feelings.
